title: Hasina names 16 December for her return from Delhi; Dhaka says she can come back 'only in handcuffs'
dek: The ousted Bangladeshi leader, sentenced to death in absentia, has asked for a state airline flight home on Victory Day. Dhaka says she must be extradited, and has put border guards on the streets of eight districts.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's ousted prime minister, plans to fly home from exile in India on 16 December, Victory Day, and has asked the Bangladeshi government to arrange her flight on the state carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines, her spokesperson said on Tuesday. It is the first time she has named a date since she fled Dhaka for Delhi on 5 August 2024.

Dhaka rejected the request within hours. "She is not a regular commercial passenger," Humaiun Kobir, a state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters at the foreign ministry on Tuesday morning. "She will have to return only in handcuffs or under strict surveillance." The government says she can come back only through extradition from India, where she has lived for more than two years. That puts the decision, and the pressure, on New Delhi.

## What happened

Hasina's spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said she "now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka", noting that she had been flown to India on a Bangladeshi aircraft in August 2024. "It is deeply symbolic that she has chosen 16 December, our Victory Day," he said in a statement. The date marks the end of the 1971 Liberation War, which her father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led. An aide, Abu Obaidha Arin, said: "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people." Earlier this month Hasina said in an interview that she would return in December "at any cost". Her claims could not be independently verified.

Mr Kobir called her "a convicted criminal; a fugitive terrorist" and said Bangladesh "will not entertain any such delusional request", according to reports. "No terrorist will ever be allowed to return this way without extradition," he told reporters. Asked about a recent string of violent attacks, he blamed what he called "Awami terrorism, sponsored by Hasina from Delhi".

Abu Abdullah M Saleh, press secretary to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, said in an interview: "My government's stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal." The government has sought her extradition, he said. The chief prosecutor of the International Crimes Tribunal, Aminul Islam, called the request for an aircraft "a ridiculous incident" and said "such a demand cannot be accepted under any circumstances". He also said that leaders of the banned Awami League who hold press conferences abroad were "effectively proving to the world" that it was "a terrorist party". An unnamed minister said on Sunday that Hasina would be arrested and jailed on arrival, and that there had been no official talks with India about an aircraft, according to reports.

## Troops on the streets

The Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said in a press release on Tuesday that it had deployed 101 platoons in Dhaka and seven other districts, Gazipur, Narayanganj, Mymensingh, Faridpur, Chattogram and Cox's Bazar, and two battalions in Gopalganj, Hasina's home district. It said the deployment, on the home ministry's instructions, was "to maintain law and order and ensure public security", and that a monitoring cell at its headquarters was watching drone and body-camera footage "round the clock". Reports differ on the number of platoons; the figure here is the BGB's own.

In Gopalganj on Monday evening, at least 30 people were injured in two clashes linked to processions by the Awami League and its affiliates, whose activities are banned, according to reports from the district. Four crude bombs went off and at least 12 shops were vandalised. Local reports traced one clash to a quarrel between youths from two villages over who stood beside party leaders at a rally, and the other to rivalry between followers of two would-be Union Parishad candidates. Police said no complaint had been filed.

## Background

Hasina ruled Bangladesh for 15 years until a student-led uprising forced her out in August 2024. The UN human rights office has said as many as 1,400 people may have been killed during the unrest. In November 2025 the International Crimes Tribunal in Dhaka sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the crackdown. She rejects the verdict and denies the charges, and a prosecutor has said she missed the deadline to appeal. Bangladesh allows presidential clemency, but she has not sought it.

The interim government led by Muhammad Yunus banned the Awami League's activities, and the party was barred from the February 2026 election. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won it, and Tarique Rahman became prime minister. Jamaat-e-Islami is now the main opposition. Violence has risen since Hasina sought a new passport and other documents earlier this month, according to reports.

India has not said whether it will hand her over. In April the Ministry of External Affairs said it was examining Bangladesh's extradition request and wanted to "engage constructively with the new government". The ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

Whatever Hasina does on 16 December, India is in the middle. Allowing her to fly to Dhaka would look to Bangladesh's government like India letting a convicted fugitive stage a political return; stopping her, or keeping her indefinitely, keeps the extradition dispute alive at a time when Delhi has said repeatedly that it wants a constructive relationship with the new government in Dhaka.

The dispute also lands on West Bengal's doorstep. On Sunday four senior Awami League leaders living in India visited the Petrapole land port in North 24 Parganas, Bangladesh's busiest trade crossing with India, and at the tribunal in Dhaka on Tuesday reporters asked whether the government had failed by letting fugitives reach border areas such as Petrapole and Agartala. Any unrest around 16 December could affect the 2,217-km Bengal stretch of the border, cross-border trade and the movement of people.

It comes as other files between the two countries are open. The 1996 Ganges Water Treaty, which governs how the river's dry-season flow at Farakka is shared, expires on 12 December, and no date has been set for renewal talks.

## What happens next

- Tuesday afternoon: Bangladesh's Minimum Wage Board resumes talks on garment workers' pay, after weeks of strikes in the industrial belt around Dhaka.
- 12 December: the Ganges Water Treaty expires.
- 16 December: Hasina's stated return date, Victory Day in Bangladesh.

The MEA's weekly briefing is the next scheduled opportunity for India to state its position.
